question: Why would you give a drug through an injection (parenterally) instead of having the patient swallow it?

options.A: It requires no special technical skill.
options.B: It achieves much faster drug absorption.
options.C: It is completely painless for the patient.
options.D: It has zero risk of local tissue damage.

explanation: You got this! Injections bypass the digestive system straight into the bloodstream or tissues, meaning the medicine gets to work much quicker. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h1)

question: Why do we have to be extra careful and double-check our work when giving injections?

options.A: Oral medications require much higher doses than injections.
options.B: Errors can cause rapid and severe harm because absorption is direct.
options.C: Hospital insurance policies mandate double-checking every dose.
options.D: The digestive system neutralizes all injectable substances.

explanation: Spot on! Once a drug is inside the body via injection, you can't take it back out. That's why accuracy is super important. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h1)

question: What is the proper technique for cleaning a patient's skin before giving an injection?

options.A: Use a circular motion starting from the center and moving outward.
options.B: Clean from the outer edges inward toward the exact puncture spot.
options.C: Wipe back and forth rapidly across the site with a dry gauze pad.
options.D: Apply warm soapy water and rinse with sterile tap water.

explanation: Well done! Starting from the center and swirling outwards pushes germs away from the exact spot where the needle will pierce the skin. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h2)

question: What is the best way to prevent accidental needlestick injuries after giving an injection?

options.A: Carefully placing the plastic cap back onto the needle using two hands.
options.B: Dropping the uncapped needle directly into a rigid sharps box.
options.C: Leaving the used syringe on the bedside table until the end of the shift.
options.D: Breaking the needle off the syringe before throwing it in the trash.

explanation: Great job! Never try to recap a used needle—that is the number one cause of accidental pricks. Drop it straight into the safety box! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h2)

question: Which of these needle gauges is the thinnest?
explanation: You rock! Remember the golden rule of needles: the higher the gauge number, the thinner the actual needle diameter. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h3)

question: Why does medication given into a muscle absorb faster than medicine given under the skin?

options.A: Muscles are located closer to the outer surface of the skin.
options.B: Intramuscular needles are always made of thinner metal.
options.C: The liver metabolizes intramuscular drugs before they enter blood vessels.
options.D: Muscle tissue has a much richer blood supply than fatty tissue.

explanation: Exactly! Muscles have a bustling network of blood vessels, helping the medication hitch a quick ride into the rest of the body. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h3)

question: What is the main reason a nurse gives an intradermal injection (just under the top layer of skin)?

options.A: Delivering rapid pain relief during acute trauma.
options.B: Providing daily maintenance doses of intravenous fluids.
options.C: Vaccinating large populations against seasonal influenza.
options.D: Diagnostic testing like allergy or tuberculosis screenings.

explanation: Spot on! Because skin layers absorb very slowly here, it's the perfect spot to watch for a localized immune reaction like a TB test. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h4)

question: When giving a routine subcutaneous insulin injection to an adult, how should you position the skin and needle?

options.A: Inject the medication directly into the dermis until a fluid bleb forms.
options.B: Push the needle straight down into the muscle at a 90-degree angle.
options.C: Stretch the skin flat and insert the needle at a 15-degree angle.
options.D: Pinch a skin fold and insert the needle at a 45 to 90-degree angle.

explanation: You got it! Pinching the fatty tissue makes sure your needle stays in the fat layer and doesn't accidentally dive into the muscle underneath. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h4)

question: Which muscle site is generally considered the safest and most reliable for giving an intramuscular injection to an adult?
explanation: Brilliant! The ventrogluteal site is clear of major nerves and big blood vessels, making it a nurse's best friend for adult IM shots. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h5)

question: What is the main benefit of using the Z-track technique when giving an intramuscular injection?

options.A: It seals the medication inside the muscle and prevents leakage into skin tissue.
options.B: It speeds up the absorption rate of irritating oily substances.
options.C: It allows the nurse to inject larger volumes of fluid into the deltoid.
options.D: It completely eliminates the pain associated with needle puncture.

explanation: Well done! Pulling the skin sideways before poking creates a zigzag path that traps irritating drugs safely down in the muscle. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h5)

question: What is the biggest clinical advantage of giving a medication straight into a vein (intravenously)?

options.A: It requires minimal monitoring compared to oral medications.
options.B: It prevents rapid allergic reactions from occurring.
options.C: It carries zero risk of localized tissue irritation.
options.D: It provides immediate systemic availability of the medication.

explanation: You're doing great! Since IV medications go right into the bloodstream, they start working instantly—a lifesaver in emergencies. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h6)

question: Why must you check if two drugs are compatible before adding an IV piggyback medicine into an existing line?

options.A: Hospital pharmacy software blocks incompatible infusions anyway.
options.B: Primary fluids neutralize the therapeutic effect of all antibiotics.
options.C: Incompatible drugs can form precipitates that block the catheter.
options.D: Mismatched drugs will automatically cause severe patient hypertension.

explanation: Spot on! Mixing the wrong drugs can cause chemical reactions that turn into solid gunk, clogging the line and endangering the patient. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h6)

question: A patient with a peripheral IV line says it hurts, and you notice the area is cool, pale, and swollen. What has likely happened?
explanation: You got it! When the IV fluid slips out of the vein and leaks into the surrounding tissue, it makes the skin feel cool, tight, and swollen. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h7)

question: Your patient suddenly starts wheezing, struggling to breathe, and breaking out in hives right after an IV medication starts. What is your very first action?

options.B: Slow the infusion rate to a keep-vein-open speed.
options.C: Notify the attending physician before taking action.
options.D: Document the vital signs in the patient chart.

explanation: Brilliant nursing instinct! Always stop the flow first to keep any more of the allergen from entering their system. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h7)

question: When is the right time for a nurse to document a medication in the patient's chart?

options.A: Only if the patient experiences a negative side effect.
options.B: Before drawing up the medication in the treatment room.
options.C: Immediately after the medication is given.
options.D: At the end of the shift during the final handover report.

explanation: Exactly right! Documenting right away prevents accidental double-dosing by another nurse who might think the dose was missed. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h8)

question: Why is it important to check up on your patient after giving an injection or IV medication?

options.A: It ensures the medication achieved its intended effect and checks for adverse reactions.
options.B: It proves to the hospital pharmacy that the correct vial was opened.
options.C: It satisfies legal billing requirements for injectable supplies.
options.D: It replaces the need to check vital signs prior to administration.

explanation: You nailed it! Because injections work fast, following up helps you catch any early side effects and make sure the patient is feeling better. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h8)
